text: Charmonium states provide a sensitive probe of the quark-gluon plasma produced in relativistic heavy-ion collisions, since color screening above the deconfinement transition is expected to modify or dissolve bound charm-anticharm pairs. In this work, we investigate the in-medium behavior of the J/ψ, χc, and ψ′ states at temperatures above the critical temperature Tc. Using a nonrelativistic potential model with a temperature-dependent heavy-quark potential constrained by lattice QCD free-energy data, we compute binding energies, radii, and dissociation temperatures for each state, and compare the resulting spectral functions with lattice correlator results. We find that the excited states melt close to the transition, whereas the J/ψ may persist as a bound state up to roughly 1.5–2 Tc, depending on the choice of potential. Implications for sequential suppression and charmonium regeneration in heavy-ion experiments are discussed.

We investigate the tunneling dynamics of a bosonic Josephson junction, realized by a Bose–Einstein condensate confined in a double-well potential, in which interwell tunneling is assisted by a single-mode optical cavity field. Within a two-mode approximation, we derive an effective Hamiltonian in which the tunneling amplitude depends on the intracavity photon number, yielding a coupled nonlinear atom–light system. Using both mean-field and full quantum treatments, we analyze the evolution of the population imbalance and the relative phase between the wells. We show that the cavity field provides a tunable control parameter that can drive transitions between Josephson oscillations and macroscopic quantum self-trapping, and that cavity-induced nonlinearity leads to bistable behavior and modified collapse-and-revival dynamics. Furthermore, the transmitted cavity field offers a nondestructive probe of the atomic tunneling dynamics.

We study the capacity of the q-ary deletion channel, in which each symbol drawn from an alphabet of size q is independently deleted with probability d, and the receiver observes the surviving symbols in order but without knowledge of their original positions. Although the binary deletion channel has been studied extensively, considerably less is known about its non-binary counterpart, and no closed-form expression for the capacity is available for any nontrivial deletion probability. In this paper, we derive a new upper bound on the capacity of the q-ary deletion channel for arbitrary q ≥ 2. Our approach builds on the technique of providing the receiver with genie-aided side information about the deletion process, which transforms the original channel into a memoryless channel whose capacity can be computed numerically using the Blahut–Arimoto algorithm. We show that the run structure of non-binary input sequences can be exploited to obtain a tighter reduction than a direct generalization of existing binary arguments. The resulting bound strictly improves on the trivial erasure-channel bound of (1 − d) log q across the full range of deletion probabilities, with the largest gains for small alphabets and high deletion rates. We further show that the gap between our bound and the erasure bound vanishes as q grows, in agreement with known asymptotic results. Numerical evaluations for several alphabet sizes illustrate the improvement over previously reported bounds.

**The Wrong Century**

The last thing Mara Okafor remembered was the lab's countdown reaching zero and someone yelling about a voltage spike. The next thing she noticed was the smell of wet straw, woodsmoke and something much worse that she later learned was a pigsty.

She sat up in a muddy field. A church bell was ringing somewhere. Two boys in rough wool tunics were staring at her from behind a stone wall, and one of them crossed himself.

Her wrist display was dead. She checked her phone and found no signal. She checked it again, which was pointless, and then laughed out loud, because the alternative was screaming.

From the shape of the church tower and the language the boys shouted as they ran, she guessed England, somewhere around the 1300s. She had studied this period for exactly one semester in college, and mainly remembered that people died of things that were easy to treat in her own time.

She learned the first lesson in the first week: knowledge is useless if you can't explain where it came from. When she tried to tell the village reeve to boil drinking water, he looked at her as if she had suggested baptizing the well. So she stopped explaining and simply did it, in front of everyone. She brewed weak ale like the locals did, since brewing involved boiling too. She washed her hands until the baker's wife started calling her "the clean woman." It wasn't meant as a compliment.

The second lesson took longer: everything is slow. Writing a letter meant finding someone who could read it. Lighting a fire took her twenty minutes and three burned fingers before old Agnes, the widow who had grudgingly taken her in, showed her how to use flint and dry fungus. Mara had once designed parts of a quantum relay. Now she was being taught by a woman who couldn't sign her own name, and Agnes was the better teacher.

There was no streaming and no scrolling, and nothing to fill the silence. The evenings were long and dark, so people talked. They told stories, sang and argued about the weather and the lord's new taxes. Mara found herself remembering more of the old songs her grandmother had taught her than she ever had in her own century, and she began to sing them by the fire. The children loved them.

She made mistakes. She nearly got herself accused of witchcraft by setting a broken arm too confidently. Only the miller's testimony, that he had seen her pray at Mass, saved her. After that she learned to frame every useful idea as something "my mother's people did," and to let others take credit when they wanted it.

By midsummer her hands had calluses. She could tell when rain was coming by the ache in the air and the way the swallows flew. She knew which herbs Agnes used for fever and which ones were just for show.

One evening in autumn, a strange shimmer appeared at the edge of the field where she had first woken, and her dead wrist display flickered on. *Retrieval window: 90 seconds.*

Mara stood in the doorway of Agnes's cottage for a long time. Then she went inside, kissed the old woman's forehead, and walked toward the light, carrying a pouch of dried yarrow she had no intention of explaining to anyone back home.

The interviews were going badly.

The first candidate, a hedge fund manager named Bradley, spent twenty minutes explaining how he would "scale suffering" and "disrupt the afterlife vertical." The Devil wrote *no* on his legal pad and underlined it twice.

The second, a former dictator, wanted to know about the dental plan. The third was a man who had once hit reply-all on a forty-thousand-person company email. The Devil respected the instinct but found him lacking in follow-through.

"They all want the fire," he told Asmodeus, his assistant of nine thousand years, as the door closed behind the dictator. "The pitchforks. The screaming. Nobody understands that the fire was never the point."

"What was the point, sir?"

The Devil rubbed his horns. He was tired. He had been tired since roughly the Renaissance. "Patience. Real torment is patient. It's quiet. It wears you down one small, reasonable-sounding obstacle at a time, until you forget you ever wanted anything."

Asmodeus checked the clipboard. "There is one more applicant. She wasn't on the list. She, ah, let herself in."

"She?"

"You did write 'man' in the posting, sir. She has filed a written objection."

The woman who entered wore a beige cardigan and a lanyard. She sat without being asked, opened a manila folder, and slid a form across the desk.

"Before we begin, you'll need to complete this," she said. "Black ink. Not blue. Blue will be rejected."

The Devil looked at the form. It was eleven pages long. Section 4 asked him to list all previous addresses, including those prior to the creation of the universe. Section 7 referred him to Section 9, which referred him back to Section 7.

"And what," he said slowly, "is your current occupation?"

"Department of Motor Vehicles. Window six. Twenty-two years." She glanced at her watch. "You'll want to take a number."

He took a number. It was 847. A small screen on the wall, which had not been there a moment ago, flickered to life: NOW SERVING 12.

For the first time in four thousand years, the Devil felt something cold slide down his spine. He looked at Asmodeus. Asmodeus, wide-eyed, nodded.

"When can you start?" the Devil asked.

She did not look up from her folder. "Your application is incomplete," she said. "Come back Tuesday."

Underwater archaeology, often called maritime or nautical archaeology when its focus is ships and seafaring, applies the principles of terrestrial fieldwork to an environment that is hostile to both people and equipment. Limited visibility, strong currents, cold, pressure and severely restricted bottom time all constrain what researchers can accomplish. Yet the same environment can preserve organic materials such as hull timbers, rope, textiles and foodstuffs that seldom survive on land. Since its emergence as a scientific discipline in the 1960s, the field has developed a sophisticated set of methods for locating, recording, recovering and conserving submerged cultural heritage.

## Locating Sites

Most investigations begin with historical research. Archival shipping records, insurance claims, old charts and reports from fishermen or sponge divers frequently narrow the search area; both the Antikythera wreck and the Late Bronze Age wreck at Uluburun, off southern Turkey, first came to light through sponge divers. Systematic survey then relies primarily on remote sensing:

- **Side-scan sonar** produces detailed acoustic images of the seabed, revealing hull outlines, ballast mounds and cargo scatters.
- **Multibeam echosounders** generate high-resolution bathymetric data from which three-dimensional terrain models can be built.
- **Sub-bottom profilers** emit lower-frequency acoustic pulses that penetrate sediment, exposing structures buried beneath the seabed.
- **Marine magnetometers** detect the magnetic anomalies produced by ferrous objects such as anchors, cannon and iron fastenings.
- **Airborne LiDAR bathymetry and satellite imagery** can map shallow, clear coastal waters across very large areas.

Targets identified in these surveys are then verified visually, either by divers or by remotely operated vehicles.

## Accessing the Site

In relatively shallow water, generally less than about 50 meters, archaeologists work directly on the seabed using SCUBA or surface-supplied air. Mixed-gas diving and closed-circuit rebreathers extend both depth and working time, albeit with greater cost, complexity and physiological risk. Beyond these limits, robotic systems are indispensable. Remotely operated vehicles (ROVs), tethered to a surface vessel, carry high-definition cameras, lighting and manipulator arms capable of delicate recovery. Autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) follow pre-programmed survey patterns, gathering sonar and photographic data across extensive areas without continuous human control. The Black Sea Maritime Archaeology Project, for example, used such technology to document dozens of wrecks in deep, oxygen-depleted water, among them a Greek merchant vessel some 2,400 years old that survives almost completely intact.

## Recording and Documentation

Because excavation is inherently destructive, meticulous recording underpins all scientific work underwater. Traditional techniques include baseline-offset measurement, trilateration from fixed control points and the use of rigid grid frames, with divers drawing on waterproof drafting film. These methods have increasingly been supplemented, and in many cases replaced, by digital approaches. Photogrammetry, or structure-from-motion, combines thousands of overlapping photographs into accurate, measurable three-dimensional models; acoustic positioning systems georeference individual finds; and underwater laser scanners capture fine surface detail. The resulting datasets permit analysis long after fieldwork has ended and allow the public to explore sites virtually.

## Excavation and Recovery

Where excavation is warranted, sediment is removed with airlifts or water dredges, which function as underwater vacuums, and the spoil is passed through sieves to recover small finds. Fragile deposits are uncovered by hand-fanning. Heavy objects are raised with lifting bags, while in shallow water a cofferdam may be constructed around a site so that it can be excavated in dry conditions, as was done for La Salle's ship *La Belle* in Texas in the 1990s. On rare occasions, entire hulls have been raised, most notably the Swedish warship *Vasa* in 1961 and Henry VIII's warship *Mary Rose* in 1982.

## Scientific Analysis

Recovered material is examined with a wide range of laboratory techniques. Dendrochronology can date ship timbers and indicate where the wood was felled, while radiocarbon dating is applied to other organic remains. Lead-isotope and elemental analyses help trace the sources of metals and ceramics, and organic residue and ancient DNA analysis can identify the former contents of amphorae. X-ray radiography and computed tomography reveal objects hidden within corrosion concretions; the latter fundamentally advanced scholarly understanding of the Antikythera Mechanism.

## Conservation

Artifacts saturated with seawater deteriorate rapidly once exposed to air, so conservation begins the moment they are lifted. Objects are kept wet and desalinated to remove soluble salts. Waterlogged wood is typically consolidated with polyethylene glycol (PEG) before being freeze-dried or slowly air-dried; *Vasa* was sprayed with PEG for seventeen years, and the conservation of the *Mary Rose* hull extended over more than three decades. Iron and copper alloys are often stabilized through electrolytic reduction.

## Preservation In Situ

The 2001 UNESCO Convention on the Protection of the Underwater Cultural Heritage establishes preservation in situ as the first option to be considered before any intervention. Accordingly, many projects now emphasize non-intrusive survey, protective reburial using sandbags or geotextiles, long-term monitoring of sediment movement and corrosion, and managed public access through underwater heritage trails. These measures respond to persistent threats, including looting, commercial trawling and the climate-related spread of wood-boring organisms.

Taken together, these methods reflect a broader evolution in the field: away from recovery as an end in itself and toward rigorous documentation, scientific interpretation and the long-term stewardship of submerged heritage.

**Nigerians Vote in Tight Presidential Race Amid Fears Over Disputed Result**

LAGOS, Nigeria — Millions of Nigerians lined up at polling stations on Saturday to choose between incumbent President Goodluck Jonathan and former military ruler Muhammadu Buhari, in what analysts say could be the most closely fought election since the country returned to civilian rule in 1999.

The vote pits Jonathan, of the long-dominant People's Democratic Party (PDP), against Buhari, a retired major general who leads the All Progressives Congress (APC), a coalition of opposition parties formed in 2013. It is the first time since the end of military rule that an opposition candidate has been widely seen as having a realistic chance of unseating a sitting president.

Voting got off to a slow start in many areas as electoral officials struggled with new biometric card readers intended to curb fraud. Jonathan himself could not be verified by a card reader at his polling unit in his home state of Bayelsa and had to be accredited manually. The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) extended voting into Sunday in some places hit by technical problems.

The election was originally scheduled for Feb. 14 but was pushed back six weeks after security chiefs said they could not guarantee safety in the northeast, where the Islamist militant group Boko Haram has waged a six-year insurgency that has killed thousands and displaced more than a million people.

Security has dominated the campaign. Buhari, who led Nigeria briefly in the 1980s after a coup, has presented himself as a disciplined leader capable of defeating the insurgents and rooting out corruption. Jonathan's supporters point to recent military gains against Boko Haram and to economic growth during his tenure, though falling oil prices have squeezed government revenues and weakened the naira.

The race also reflects Nigeria's long-standing regional and religious divides. Buhari, a Muslim, draws much of his support from the predominantly Muslim north, while Jonathan, a Christian, is strongest in the south, including the oil-producing Niger Delta.

Those divisions have fueled concern that the losing side may refuse to accept the result. After the 2011 election, in which Jonathan defeated Buhari, rioting in parts of the north left around 800 people dead, according to Human Rights Watch.

In January, both candidates signed an accord in Abuja pledging to campaign peacefully and respect the outcome, but tensions have remained high. Some militants in the Niger Delta have warned of unrest if Jonathan loses, while some Buhari supporters have vowed to resist any result they consider rigged.

International observers, including teams from the African Union and the European Union, are monitoring the vote, and world leaders have urged Nigerians to keep the process peaceful.

INEC chairman Attahiru Jega has said results will be collated at the state level before being announced in Abuja, with official figures expected in the coming days.

To win outright, a candidate needs a simple majority of votes nationwide and at least 25 percent of the vote in two-thirds of Nigeria's 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory.

The Earth's rotation does not directly affect flight duration. The atmosphere rotates along with the planet, so an aircraft moves relative to a body of air that is already traveling at essentially the same speed as the surface below. Consequently, an eastbound aircraft gains no advantage from the Earth "turning beneath it," and a westbound aircraft incurs no penalty.

Rotation does, however, exert an important indirect influence. Together with the temperature contrast between the equator and the poles, the Coriolis effect arising from the Earth's rotation helps generate the jet streams: fast, west-to-east currents of air in the upper atmosphere. At mid-latitudes, eastbound flights can take advantage of these tailwinds, whereas westbound flights must fly into them. For this reason, a flight from New York to London is typically about an hour shorter than the return journey.

## Overview

Arctic Silver and Thermal Grizzly take different approaches to thermal interface materials. Arctic Silver, an American manufacturer, is best known for Arctic Silver 5, a long-established silver-filled compound. Thermal Grizzly, based in Germany, offers a wider performance-oriented range, from conventional pastes to liquid metal. Note that Arctic Silver is a separate company from **ARCTIC** (maker of the MX series), and the two are often confused.

## Thermal Conductivity

| Product | Type | Manufacturer-rated conductivity | Electrically conductive |
|---|---|---|---|
| Arctic Silver 5 | Silver-filled paste | Not officially stated in W/m·K (third-party figures of roughly 8–9 W/m·K are commonly cited) | No (slightly capacitive) |
| Arctic Silver Céramique 2 | Ceramic paste | Not officially stated in W/m·K | No |
| Thermal Grizzly Aeronaut | Paste | 8.5 W/m·K | No |
| Thermal Grizzly Hydronaut | Paste | 11.8 W/m·K | No |
| Thermal Grizzly Kryonaut | Paste | 12.5 W/m·K | No |
| Thermal Grizzly Kryonaut Extreme | Paste | 14.2 W/m·K | No |
| Thermal Grizzly Conductonaut | Liquid metal | 73 W/m·K | **Yes** |

Manufacturers do not measure conductivity under a common standard, so published figures are not directly comparable. Independent testing generally shows that premium non-metallic pastes perform within a few degrees Celsius of one another. Liquid metal is the clear exception and can offer substantially lower temperatures where it is appropriate.

## Curing Time

- **Arctic Silver 5:** The manufacturer specifies a break-in period of roughly 200 hours under normal thermal cycling, during which temperatures may fall by a few degrees. Initial measurements may therefore understate its eventual performance.
- **Thermal Grizzly pastes (Kryonaut, Hydronaut, Aeronaut):** No meaningful curing period. They perform at or near their peak right after installation, which helps with benchmarking and with short-term overclocking sessions.
- **Conductonaut:** No curing period. However, liquid metal can be absorbed into or react with some metals over time, so occasional inspection is advisable.

## Application Method

- **Arctic Silver 5** has a relatively thick consistency. The manufacturer recommends a line or small dot, depending on the processor's die layout, followed by even mounting pressure. Because it is slightly capacitive, contact with exposed circuitry should still be avoided.
- **Kryonaut and Hydronaut** spread easily and suit the dot, line, or spread method. Kryonaut's lower viscosity also makes it convenient for manual spreading.
- **Kryonaut Extreme** is thicker and better suited to large, flat surfaces and to the demanding contact conditions of extreme overclocking.
- **Conductonaut** must be applied in a very thin layer with the supplied applicator or swab. It is electrically conductive and reacts with aluminum, so nearby surface-mount components should be insulated (for example, with conformal coating or Kapton tape), and it must never be used with aluminum heatsink bases.

## Choosing for Specific Use Cases

**High-end overclocking:** Kryonaut or Kryonaut Extreme is generally preferred for ambient and sub-ambient overclocking because neither needs curing and both perform well under high heat flux. Note that Kryonaut is reported to degrade faster at sustained high temperatures, especially on GPUs. For a daily-use system, a pump-out-resistant paste or a periodic reapplication schedule is advisable.

**Low-profile coolers:** Compact coolers typically provide lower mounting pressure and have less thermal headroom. An easily spreadable, non-conductive paste such as Hydronaut or Kryonaut ensures a thin bond line under limited pressure. Arctic Silver 5 is also a reasonable, economical choice if the user accepts its break-in period.

**Delidded CPUs:** Conductonaut is the established choice between the die and the integrated heat spreader, where its high conductivity delivers the greatest improvement. Between the heat spreader and the cooler, a conventional paste such as Kryonaut is usually recommended to limit risk. Users should confirm that the IHS and cooler surfaces are copper or nickel-plated copper, and should expect some staining.

## Summary

For general builds where cost and longevity matter, Arctic Silver 5 remains a dependable option. For immediate peak performance and enthusiast applications, Thermal Grizzly's range offers more flexibility. Liquid metal should be reserved for experienced users working with delidded or direct-die configurations.

When an investor turned down Jia Jiang's startup idea in 2012, the rejection hurt so much that he nearly abandoned his dream of becoming an entrepreneur. Instead, he decided to get used to hearing "no."

Jiang, who moved from China to the United States as a teenager, gave himself a challenge: every day for 100 days, he would make a request he expected to be refused, and he would film each attempt.

The requests were deliberately unusual. He asked a stranger to lend him $100. He asked a burger restaurant for a "burger refill." He asked to play soccer in a stranger's backyard.

Then, on day three, he walked into a Krispy Kreme and asked for doughnuts linked together like the Olympic rings. To his astonishment, the employee made them. The video spread rapidly online, drawing millions of views, and "100 Days of Rejection" suddenly had a global audience.

What began as personal therapy turned into an unexpected career. Jiang wrote a book, "Rejection Proof," delivered a popular TED talk and now speaks to audiences about overcoming fear.

The experiment pushed him far outside his comfort zone, but it taught him that rejection itself is rarely as painful as people imagine. What really holds us back, Jiang concluded, is the fear of rejection — the dread of hearing "no" that keeps many people from asking at all.

Along the way, he discovered something else: when he asked, people said "yes" far more often than he expected.

**'American Pie' Lyrics Fetch $1.2 Million at Auction**

NEW YORK — The original manuscript of Don McLean's "American Pie," one of the most dissected songs in American popular music, sold for $1.2 million at Christie's in New York on Tuesday.

The 16-page manuscript, which includes McLean's handwritten and typed drafts of the lyrics along with his working notes, went to an unidentified buyer.

For more than four decades, fans and critics have debated the meaning of the song's dense, symbol-laden verses, which feature a jester, a king and queen, a marching band and the famous line about "the day the music died." That phrase is widely understood to refer to the 1959 plane crash that killed Buddy Holly, Ritchie Valens and J.P. "The Big Bopper" Richardson.

McLean has generally declined to explain the song line by line, but he has said the lyrics and notes being sold would reveal its meaning to anyone willing to study them. He has described the song in broad terms as a reflection on an America he felt was drifting in the wrong direction as the optimism of the 1950s gave way to the upheaval of the 1960s.

Released in 1971, the eight-and-a-half-minute ballad is McLean's biggest hit. It reached No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 in January 1972 and stayed there for four weeks, and it remains a fixture on classic rock radio.

The sale ranks among the highest prices ever paid at auction for song lyrics.

Should Companies Track Employees Online?

Most people would agree that a company has the right to protect its own computers. However, I believe tracking should be limited and honest.

Companies do have good reasons to watch some online activity. Hackers often get into businesses through employees who open bad links or visit unsafe websites. Monitoring helps catch these problems early and keeps customer information safe. It can also stop people from using work time for things that are clearly inappropriate.

On the other hand, too much tracking hurts workers. If every click and keystroke is recorded, employees may feel like they are not trusted, and this can make them stressed and less motivated. Workers also deserve some privacy, even at work.

In my opinion, companies should be allowed to track online activity only for safety and security, and they must tell employees exactly what is being watched. That way, businesses stay protected and workers are treated with respect.

Should Companies Watch What Workers Do Online?

Today almost every job use computers and the internet. Because of this, many companies want to know what their workers are doing online during work time. Some people think this is normal, but other people think it is not fair. In my opinion, companies can track some things, but they should not watch everything.

First, I understand why companies want to check. The company pays the workers to do their job, not to watch videos or shopping online all day. If a worker spend three hours on social media, the boss is losing money. Also, there is a big problem with safety on the internet. Sometimes a worker clicks on a bad email and a virus come into the computer. Then hackers can steal important information about customers. So the company need some control to protect itself.

But on the other side, too much tracking is not good. I have a friend who work in an office where the company take pictures of the screen every ten minutes. She told me she feel nervous all the time, like somebody is always behind her. She cannot relax, and she said she actually work slower because of the stress. I think people need a little bit of trust to do a good job. When the boss checks every small thing, workers feel like children or like criminals.

Also, privacy is important for everybody. Sometimes a person needs to check a message from the doctor or from their child's school during work. This is private information, and the boss should not read it. If the company see everything, they can learn things about workers that is not their business, for example about health or family problems.

So what is the best answer? I think there must be clear rules. The company should tell workers before what they will check and why. For example, they can block dangerous websites and check for viruses, this is fair. But they should not read personal messages or record every key the workers press. And the information should be only for security, not for punish people for small things like a five-minute break.

In conclusion, companies have some good reasons to track online activity, especially for safety. But they must be honest and not go too far. A good workplace needs both security and trust. If the company respect the workers, the workers will also respect the company and work harder.

Subject: Verbal confirmation for direct trades

Hi everyone,

Effective [date], all direct trades, meaning those executed bilaterally with a counterparty rather than through a broker or an electronic platform, must be verbally confirmed before they are booked.

Over the past few months, we've had several disputes over price and volume on direct deals. In every case, the problem would have been caught by a quick confirmation call. Brokered and electronic trades come with an independent record of the terms; direct trades don't, which means accuracy is entirely on us.

Going forward, please:

1. Call the counterparty on a recorded line to confirm terms immediately after execution, and in no case more than 30 minutes after the trade.
2. Read back all key terms: counterparty, buy/sell, product, volume, price, delivery point or settlement terms, and start and end dates.
3. Note the name of the person you spoke with and the time of the call on the deal ticket.
4. If any term doesn't match, hold off on booking the trade and escalate to [Name] in middle office right away.

This step is in addition to, not a replacement for, the written confirmation process. The confirmations group will continue sending written confirms as usual.

I know this adds a minute or two to each deal. It's still far less time than we've spent unwinding disputes after the fact, and it protects both us and our counterparties.

If you have questions or see practical problems with the process, send them my way by [date] so we can sort them out before it takes effect.

Thank you,
[Your Name]

**Zayn Malik Quits One Direction, Leaving Fans Heartbroken**

Zayn Malik has left One Direction, saying he wants to live as "a normal 22-year-old" away from the relentless spotlight of one of the world's biggest boy bands.

The announcement, posted on the band's official Facebook page on Wednesday, confirmed that the remaining four members, Harry Styles, Niall Horan, Liam Payne and Louis Tomlinson, will continue as a quartet and complete their ongoing world tour.

"My life with One Direction has been more than I could ever have imagined," Malik said in the statement. "But, after five years, I feel like now is the right time for me to leave the band."

The news set off an outpouring of grief online. Within hours, hashtags expressing devotion to the singer were trending worldwide, and fans posted videos of themselves in tears. Some said they had stayed home from school or work to process the news. Malik had already left the tour days earlier, citing stress.

While many parents may be tempted to dismiss the reaction as melodrama, child psychologists say the moment should be taken seriously, and used constructively.

"For a lot of young fans, this is their first experience of loss involving something they've invested in emotionally," one family therapist said. "It's a real feeling, and it's a safe opportunity for parents to talk about how we cope when things change."

Experts recommend that parents listen rather than mock, acknowledge their child's sadness, and gently point out that disappointment passes. Learning to bounce back from small heartbreaks, they say, builds the resilience children will need for bigger ones later in life.

# Asia's Richest Man Builds a $193 Million Monastery — Complete With Bulletproof VIP Rooms

HONG KONG — A lavish Buddhist monastery financed by Li Ka-shing, Asia's richest man, will open to the public by mid-April, offering visitors a close-up view of one of the largest statues of the Goddess of Mercy ever built — and, for a privileged few, rooms protected by bulletproof glass.

Tsz Shan Monastery, whose name translates roughly as "Mountain of Compassion," sits on a green hillside in Tai Po, in Hong Kong's New Territories. The complex cost about HK$1.5 billion, or $193 million, and was paid for through the tycoon's charitable foundation after years of planning and construction.

Towering over the grounds is a gleaming white bronze statue of Guan Yin, the bodhisattva of compassion revered across East Asia. At 76 meters (about 250 feet), it is believed to be the second-tallest Guan Yin statue in the world, surpassed only by a 108-meter figure in Sanya, on China's southern island province of Hainan.

The monastery's more worldly touches have drawn just as much attention. Its VIP rooms are reported to be fitted with bulletproof windows, a feature more often associated with embassies than with places of meditation. The precaution may reflect the high-profile guests the monastery expects to receive, as well as the security concerns that come with being tied to one of the world's wealthiest men.

Li, 86, built an empire spanning ports, property, telecommunications and retail, and his fortune is estimated at more than $30 billion. He is also one of Hong Kong's most prominent philanthropists and has famously described his foundation as his "third son," pledging a third of his assets to it.

Visitors won't pay to get in, but they won't be able to simply turn up, either. Entry will be handled through an online booking system, with daily numbers capped to keep the grounds peaceful. Organizers have said they want Tsz Shan to remain a place for reflection and the study of Buddhism rather than another stop on the city's crowded tourist circuit.

That would set it apart from Hong Kong's best-known Buddhist landmark, the 34-meter Tian Tan Buddha on Lantau Island, which draws busloads of sightseers every day.

Whether a monastery with a 76-meter goddess and bulletproof glass can stay off the tourist map remains to be seen. For now, anyone hoping to see Guan Yin up close will need to book ahead.

1. **Smash it on toast.** Spread mashed avocado on toasted sourdough and top it with flaky salt, chili flakes, a squeeze of lemon, and a fried or jammy egg if you want.

2. **Make guacamole.** Mash it with lime juice, diced onion, cilantro, jalapeño, and salt. Fold in chopped tomato just before serving.

3. **Blend it into a smoothie.** Half an avocado with banana, spinach, and milk or yogurt makes a thick, creamy smoothie that keeps you full longer.

4. **Turn it into a pasta sauce.** Blend avocado with garlic, basil, lemon juice, olive oil, and a splash of pasta water for a quick no-cook sauce.

5. **Bake it into chocolate mousse.** Blend avocado with cocoa powder, maple syrup or honey, vanilla, and a pinch of salt, then chill it. The avocado flavor disappears and you're left with a rich, silky dessert.

One quick note before the list: Mariya Takeuchi debuted in 1978, so she does belong to the late-70s scene, but most of her best-known songs actually come from the 1980s and later. Her career has lasted more than four decades, and her signature sound sits at the center of what is now called "city pop." The songs below cover her whole career, with the 1970s material marked so you can focus on it if your assignment requires.

## Late 1970s – Early 1980s (RCA years)

**"Modotte Oide, Watashi no Jikan" (1978)**
Her debut single. It's a breezy, polished pop song that introduced her as a college-aged singer with a clear, warm voice. Not her biggest hit, but important as the start of her career.

**"September" (1979)**
One of her signature early songs, written by Takao Kisugi with lyrics by Takashi Matsumoto. It's a bittersweet song about a relationship fading as summer turns to autumn. It earned her wide recognition and remains a fan favorite.

**"Watashi no Heart wa Stop Motion" (1979)**
An upbeat single used in a cosmetics commercial, which helped make her a household name. It shows the bright, idol-adjacent side of her early image.

**"Fushigi na Peach Pie" (1980)**
Probably her biggest hit of the RCA era. Also tied to a cosmetics campaign, it's playful and catchy, with a sunny pop arrangement. If you need one song to represent her earliest fame, this is a strong choice.

**"Sweetest Music" (1980)**
From the album *Miss M*, which was partly recorded in Los Angeles with American session musicians. The song reflects how closely her sound was linked to West Coast AOR at the time.

## Mid-1980s (after her marriage to Tatsuro Yamashita)

In 1982 she married musician and producer Tatsuro Yamashita, took a break from performing, and returned as a songwriter who wrote most of her own material. Yamashita produced and arranged much of her later work.

**"Plastic Love" (1984)**
From the album *Variety*. This is now her most famous song worldwide. It was only a modest success on release, but around 2017 an unofficial upload on YouTube went viral, and the song became the face of the global city pop revival. Its funky bassline, disco-influenced groove and lonely lyrics about a woman who hides her heartbreak in nightlife have been endlessly covered and remixed.

**"Mou Ichido" (1984)**
Another single from *Variety*, a mid-tempo ballad that showed her growing strength as a songwriter.

**"Genki wo Dashite" (1984 / 1987)**
She originally wrote this for actress-singer Hiroko Yakushimaru, then recorded her own version on the album *Request* (1987). It's a gentle, encouraging song telling a friend to cheer up after a breakup, and it's one of her most beloved tracks in Japan.

## Late 1980s – 1990s

**"Single Again" (1989)**
A dramatic ballad about running into a former lover after both of their lives have changed. It was used as a TV drama theme and became one of her biggest commercial hits.

**"Kokuhaku" (1990)**
Another drama-linked ballad, emotionally heavy and very popular, continuing her success with mature love songs.

**"Junai Rhapsody" (1994)**
A major hit that was included on the compilation *Impressions*, which sold several million copies and is one of the best-selling albums in Japanese history.

**"Camouflage" (1998)**
Used as the theme for a TV drama, this song topped the Oricon charts and showed that she was still commercially strong two decades after her debut.

## 2000s and Later

**"Inochi no Uta" (2008 / 2012)**
Originally written for an NHK drama under a pen name, this song about gratitude for life later became widely known in her own recording and is often sung at ceremonies in Japan.

**Recent albums**
*Denim* (2007), *Trad* (2014) and *Precious Days* (2024) show she has kept releasing new material, though she rarely tours.

## Suggestions for Your Assignment

- If the focus is strictly the 1970s, use "Modotte Oide, Watashi no Jikan," "September," and "Watashi no Heart wa Stop Motion," and mention "Fushigi na Peach Pie" as the 1980 peak of that period.
- If the focus is her overall popularity, "Plastic Love," "Single Again," and "Genki wo Dashite" are essential.
- If the focus is cultural impact, "Plastic Love" is the key case study, since its online rediscovery is a good example of how the internet revived interest in older Japanese pop for an international audience.

**Serena Williams' Longtime Hitting Partner Joins Azarenka's Camp**

Serena Williams has parted ways with Sascha Bajin, the hitting partner who spent eight years helping prepare the world No. 1 for some of the biggest matches of her career.

Bajin has resurfaced in the camp of Victoria Azarenka, the former world No. 1 from Belarus and one of Williams' most persistent rivals on the WTA Tour.

The split appears to have happened before the start of the season. Bajin was absent from Melbourne this year as Williams captured the Australian Open, her 19th Grand Slam singles title. The win moved her past Chris Evert and Martina Navratilova on the all-time list and left her three short of Steffi Graf's Open Era record of 22.

Neither Williams nor Bajin has publicly explained the move. Hitting partners rarely draw attention outside the locker room, but they play an outsized role behind the scenes, mimicking opponents' patterns in practice, absorbing hours of drills and often serving as a sounding board during long stretches on the road.

For Azarenka, the addition is a coup. Her coach, Wim Fissette, said he was thrilled to bring Bajin into the team, praising his experience at the highest level of the sport and his familiarity with what it takes to win major titles.

Azarenka, a two-time Australian Open champion, is working her way back toward the top of the rankings after an injury-plagued 2014. Fissette, who previously coached Kim Clijsters and Simona Halep, joined her late last year.

Bajin's insight into Williams' game could prove useful if the two meet again. Azarenka has lost most of their matches, including two US Open finals.

Dr. Peter Albright delivered the news the way some men hand out parking tickets: briskly, and with the faint air of having done her a favor.

"Six months," he said. "Perhaps less. I'd get your affairs in order, Mrs. Kowalczyk."

Edna Kowalczyk was eighty-one. She had buried a husband, two dogs, and a forty-year fondness for menthol cigarettes. She looked down at Dr. Albright's loafers, which had tassels, and decided right then that she would not be giving him the satisfaction.

"I'll see you in six months," she said.

"I'd hope so," he replied, already reaching for the next chart.

She went home and made a list. It was not a list of affairs to put in order. It was titled THINGS ALBRIGHT WILL HAVE TO HEAR ABOUT, and the first item was *Walk to the mailbox without the cane.*

It took three weeks. Her hip complained the entire time, and she told her hip, out loud, that it could take its complaints to Dr. Albright.

The second item was the county fair, where she intended to enter her rhubarb pie for the first time since 1997. The third was learning to use the tablet her granddaughter had given her, because she had heard you could leave reviews of doctors on the internet.

At the six-month appointment, Dr. Albright frowned at her bloodwork for a very long time.

"Well," he said. "This is unusual."

"Second place," Edna said. "For the pie. The woman who won is married to one of the judges. I'm appealing."

He didn't know what to say to that, so he told her to come back in three months.

She came back in three months. And three after that. Her granddaughter, Talia, started driving her to the appointments because she wanted to watch. Edna would sit bolt upright on the crinkly paper, Dr. Albright would study her numbers as though they had personally insulted him, and Talia would bite the inside of her cheek to keep from laughing.

"What's your secret?" a nurse asked her once in the hallway.

"Pettiness," Edna said. "Wildly underrated."

It wasn't the whole truth. There was also the pie, which took first place the following year, after the judge's wife retired. There was the tablet, on which she discovered Talia had been posting photos of her with captions like *my grandma is undefeated*. There was the spring she planted tomatoes she had no business expecting to eat, and ate them anyway, warm from the vine, with a little salt.

But spite was what had gotten her out of the chair that first morning, and Edna believed in giving credit where it was due.

Four years after the six-month prognosis, Dr. Albright announced his retirement. Edna sent a card. Inside, in careful cursive, she wrote: *Congratulations. I'll be here when you get back.*

Talia asked whether that was a little mean.

"Sweetheart," Edna said, cutting her a slice of pie, "it's a lot mean. That's the whole point."
